# Perdition Gulch

## I.

The parcel in question was eleven acres of scrub grass running along the eastern bank of Perdition Creek, which in June of that year held approximately four inches of brown water and the bleached skeleton of a mule. Two men claimed it. Harlan Moss said he'd bought it from a Paiute who had no right to sell it. William Fane said he'd shaken hands with Harlan Oss's father on a different boundary, one that put the creek entirely on the Fane side, and that the handshake had been witnessed by no one living.

Maren Calloway sat in the chair they'd given her on the east side of the claims office, a room that smelled of pine resin and tobacco spit. She was forty-six. Her hair was the color of creek sand and she kept it pinned in a manner that suggested she had once cared about the pinning and had not updated the habit since. She had not been asked to speak. She sat with her hands folded on the table in front of her and waited for the two men to exhaust themselves, which took the better part of an hour.

When they were finished, she said: "On the fourteenth of March, 1862, Harlan Moss Sr. and William Fane Sr. stood at the southwest corner post—the one with the notch cut in it, Mr. Fane, the one you used to hang your canteen from when you were small—and Amos Moss said, 'The water is yours up to the bend where the cottonwood fell in the storm of '58, and past that it is mine, and we will not speak of it again.' And your father said, 'That suits me, Amos, though I think you are a fool for wanting the east section when the graze is better on the west.' And they shook hands, and your father wiped his palm on his trousers afterward because Amos Moss had been eating a peach."

Neither man spoke.

"The cottonwood that fell," Maren said, "is still there. Its root structure is visible at low water. It is approximately two hundred yards north of the boundary Mr. Moss has described and approximately forty yards south of the boundary Mr. Fane has described. Both of you are wrong and both of your fathers are dead. I suggest you go find the tree."

They went to find the tree. They found it. The dispute ended.

---

The night sky over the settlement at Rios Piedras held no moon, and the riders came from the south in a column of eight. They moved at a walk. None of them spoke. The first lantern in the settlement was lit in the window of a house belonging to a family named Soto—a woman, her husband, three children, the youngest seven months old. The lantern was lit because the baby had been fussing.

Maren Calloway watched from the ridge. She was three hundred yards from the settlement and could see the riders and the lanterns and the exact topography of the arroyo that ran behind the eastern houses—the arroyo that, if the Sotos moved now, immediately, out the back door along the goat path to the place where the bank dropped low enough for a woman carrying an infant to scramble down—

She calculated the route in the time it takes to blink. Every foot of it. The angle of cover, the depth of shadow, the distance to the tree line. She saw it the way she saw everything: completely, instantly, and forever.

She did not move.

---

Thomas Pfeil, whom the town called the doctor though he had no degree and no instruments beyond a leather case of needles and catgut, sat on the stool in his office on Perdition Gulch's one real street and sutured the wound in his own left side with the steady hand of a man threading a needle by lamplight, which is precisely what he was doing. The wound was four inches long and deep enough to show the pearlescent fascia over his ribs. An hour ago it had been a knife, held by a man whose name was Edgar Bly, aimed at the back of a woman named Sarah Kopp who had refused to sell Edgar Bly her late husband's claim. Thomas had stepped between them in the street with the economical motion of someone who has been stepping between blades and bodies for a long time. The knife went in and Edgar Bly looked at Thomas's face—which registered nothing, not pain, not shock, only a flat diagnostic attention—and Edgar Bly ran.

Now Thomas pulled the catgut tight. The wound's edges met. By morning they would be a pink line. By the following evening, nothing. His body repaired itself the way a river fills a hole: relentlessly, without intention, because the physics demanded it.

He knotted the suture anyway, out of habit, or perhaps out of a desire to pretend the repair required effort.

---

The eighth rider in the column carried a scattergun across his saddle horn. Thomas Pfeil stood sixty yards from the settlement, close enough to hear the horses, close enough to smell them. He was twenty-two years old and had already survived a wound that should have killed him—a fall onto a broken fencepost at fifteen that had driven a splinter of cedar through his left lung. He had lain in a ditch for six hours and felt his body knit itself shut around the foreign object, and he had pulled the splinter out through the hole it had entered and watched the hole seal like water closing over a dropped stone.

He knew what the scattergun would do to an ordinary man's chest. He knew what it would do to his. The same thing the fencepost had done: nothing that lasted.

He could walk into the column. He could stand in front of the Sotos' door. The pellets would enter him and his body would push them out like seeds from wet soil, and the riders would see this, and they would understand that something was in front of them that they could not kill, and some of them—most of them—would turn their horses.

He would be seen.

He stayed where he was. The sound the scattergun made, when it finally discharged into the Sotos' front door, was flat and unimpressive, like a book dropped on a wood floor.

---

The child's name was Dessa. She was eleven years old and had not spoken above a whisper in anyone's memory. The sheriff of Perdition Gulch, a man named Boone who had survived the war and its aftermath and who had adopted a policy, in the years since, of believing approximately nothing he could not verify by direct observation, nonetheless believed the child because the child had never once been wrong.

On a Tuesday in August, Dessa walked to the sheriff's office and stood in the doorway, blocking the light, and whispered: "Lyle Pardee is going to take Mr. Hoffman's four best steers tonight. He will use the north road and he will have a man with him named Coates who has a pistol with a filed sight. They have not saddled their horses yet. They are in the back room of the Yellow House playing cards and talking about it."

Boone looked at her. "How do you know this, Dessa."

Dessa looked at a point slightly to the left of Boone's face, the way she always did, as if direct eye contact was a frequency her equipment could not process. "They are thinking about it," she said. "Mr. Pardee is thinking about the money. Mr. Coates is thinking about his pistol. He is worried it will misfire. He is right to worry. The spring is bad."

Boone rode to the Yellow House and found Lyle Pardee and a man named Coates in the back room, playing cards. He arrested them for conspiracy to commit theft. In Coates's belt was a pistol with a filed sight. The spring was, in fact, bad. It misfired when Boone tested it behind the jail. The bullet went into the dirt at an angle that would have, had anyone been standing where a man being robbed of his cattle might reasonably stand, struck that man in the thigh.

No one asked Boone how he had known. In Perdition Gulch, people had learned not to ask how things were known. They understood, in the way that organisms understand the presence of a current in water, that the town operated according to principles that were not available to them and that the principles, thus far, had kept them alive.

---

Dessa sat in the dark behind the livery stable in Rios Piedras and pressed her palms against her ears, though this accomplished nothing, had never accomplished anything, because the sound was not sound.

The woman in the Soto house was thinking about the stove. She had lit it before the baby woke and now she could not remember if she had closed the flue and she was thinking, with the very specific anxiety of a woman who has been tired for seven months, *I will burn the house down, I am always forgetting, Luis will be angry—*

The man beside her was trying to remember a prayer. He was a Catholic and he had been a Catholic all his life and the prayer was the Ave Maria and he could not remember the words past *gratia plena* and he was thinking, with a fury that was indistinguishable from grief, *I have said this ten thousand times, I have said this every day, God will not hear a man who cannot remember—*

The seven-month-old was thinking nothing that could be rendered in language. The seven-month-old was experiencing a sensation of sudden brightness and noise and the withdrawal of warmth and the absence of the heartbeat that had been, moments ago, pressed against the baby's cheek, and the baby's entire cognitive apparatus was devoted to a single unword that meant: *where.*

Dessa heard all of it. She heard the older children, who thought in pictures—the girl thinking of a yellow dog she had played with that morning, the boy thinking of a crack in the ceiling that looked like a horse, both of these images stuttering, fragmenting, and going out like lamps in a wind. She heard the riders' thoughts too, which were mostly practical and mostly dull—a man thinking about money, a man thinking about his saddle sore, a man thinking about a woman in Prescott—and the dullness of the killers' thoughts against the brilliance of the dying's was the most obscene thing Dessa had ever encountered and she would encounter it for the rest of her life, every time she closed her eyes, because she was eleven years old and she did not yet know that some frequencies, once received, transmit forever.

She could have screamed. A scream from the ridge, a child's scream, would have been something—a handful of seconds, a door opened, a family running for the arroyo. She knew this. She felt Maren beside her, Maren who had already calculated the route. She felt Thomas somewhere behind them, Thomas whose body was a wall no bullet could breach. She felt the twins, Isla and Cora, on opposite ends of the ridge, their shared mind already modeling the scenario: if one of them ran north and the other south, the riders would split, confused by movement on two flanks, and in the gap—

Five glances in the dark. Five calculations arriving at the same conclusion from five different sets of impossible data.

If they acted, they would be seen. If they were seen, they would be known. If they were known, the world would not permit them to continue as they were—five people who looked human but were not, not entirely, not in any way the world had a framework to forgive.

The riders entered the settlement. The sounds that followed were not remarkable. History is mostly composed of unremarkable sounds heard by people who chose, for their own reasons, to be elsewhere.

Maren remembered everything. Thomas's body did not mark itself. Dessa heard the last thought of the last Soto—the boy, who was six, and who thought, at the end, about the crack in the ceiling, because the mind in extremity returns to the thing it was holding, and he had been holding a horse made of plaster and shadow, and then he was not.

The twins looked at each other across sixty yards of darkness, which was, for them, no distance at all. They did not need to speak. They did not need to think. They shared a single set of feelings and those feelings contained, in that moment, a relief so deep and so sickening that neither of them, in the years that followed, ever once referred to the night at Rios Piedras. They didn't need to. They both already knew.

---

On a Thursday in September, the railroad surveyor Arthur Comstock arrived in Perdition Gulch to discuss the terms under which the Perdition Creek spur line would enter the town. He was met at the edge of town by Isla Fenn. He was met at his hotel by Cora Fenn. He did not know they were sisters. They looked nothing alike—Isla sharp-faced and dark, Cora wide and fair, a genetic distribution so asymmetrical that no one who had not watched them born from the same body would have supposed a connection.

Isla sat with Comstock over coffee in the hotel's single public room and discussed the right-of-way along the northern parcels. She asked precise questions about the railroad's survey methodology, its timetable, its financing structure. Comstock found her intelligent. He told her more than he intended.

Two hours later, in the claims office, Cora met him with a summary of the northern parcel owners' concerns. The summary addressed, point by point, every piece of information Comstock had shared with Isla. It anticipated his counterarguments. It named the specific concessions the railroad's financing structure could absorb. Comstock had not discussed these matters with anyone in Perdition Gulch except the sharp-faced woman at the hotel, and the wide, fair woman in front of him seemed to have no connection to that conversation, and yet she knew—

He felt outflanked. He felt as though he were negotiating with someone who had read his notes.

He agreed to route the spur line along the southern boundary, sparing six families the destruction of their properties. He left Perdition Gulch that evening with the insoluble feeling a chess player feels when he realizes, too late, that his opponent saw the entire board.

In separate rooms on opposite sides of the town's one street, Isla and Cora Fenn each poured a glass of water at the same moment, drank at the same rate, set the glass down with the same motion of the wrist. Neither noticed, in the way that a heart does not notice its beating.

---

This was the machinery. Five hands on five ropes, and the knot holding, and the town hanging suspended over the gorge it was named for. There is a temptation, in describing such an arrangement, to call it order, or governance, or even justice. A land survey does not use these words. A land survey notes the location of boundaries, the presence of structures, the angle of slopes and the depth of wells. The survey of Perdition Gulch, if one were conducted, would show a town of 340 souls arrayed along a single street in a high desert valley, dependent on a creek that was dry five months of the year and a rail connection that did not yet exist, protected from the routine entropy of the frontier by five individuals whose methods were opaque and whose authority derived from no election, no statute, and no god.

The survey would not show the Soto family. The survey would not show Rios Piedras, which was fifty miles south and had been abandoned for six years and was slowly being reclaimed by creosote and wind. The survey would not show the precise shape of the silence that existed between the five members of the council when they sat together on the porch of the claims office on Sunday evenings, watching the light fail, saying nothing, because everything that needed to be said between them had been said by their five separate decisions not to act on a night when eight riders came from the south, and the saying of it had taken no words at all.

The survey would show a town that functioned. That is all a survey is for.

---

## II.

The cut was on the outside of his left forearm, just below the elbow. He had opened it on the edge of a tin pail in his office—a careless motion, reaching for a roll of bandage on the high shelf, his arm catching the pail's lip as it passed. A wound so trivial it did not deserve the word. A scratch. A parting of the skin no longer than a thumb.

Thomas Pfeil cleaned it, out of habit, and wrapped it, out of habit, and went to sleep.

In the morning, the bandage was spotted brown. He unwrapped it. The cut was still open. Its edges were pink and slightly swollen, the way a cut looks on a person whose body obeys the ordinary schedule of damage and repair—the way a cut had not looked on Thomas Pfeil's body since he was fourteen years old.
